summary.text: Mark Eugenikos is remembered as an Orthodox opponent of the union concluded at Florence. His life is particularly important for understanding the difference between participation in a council and acceptance of its final doctrinal settlement.

blocks.text: The cathedral account calls him Emmanuel, born at Constantinople in 1392. After his father’s death he continues his education, becomes a teacher, and later chooses monastic life with the name Mark. His theological reputation precedes his episcopal appointment.

blocks.text: At Ferrara and Florence the cathedral biography follows his arguments about purgatory and disputed Latin teachings. It depicts an initially conciliatory participant who refuses a settlement he believes compromises the Orthodox confession. The rhetoric and interpretation belong to that Orthodox biography.

blocks.text: Mouravieff’s nineteenth-century history places Mark’s opposition alongside the Russian metropolitan Isidore’s support for the union. It names disputes over the procession of the Holy Spirit, purgatory, eucharistic bread, and papal authority. The author emphasizes the Byzantine empire’s desperate political situation and the hope of Western assistance. In that narrative Mark refuses the council’s acts, while Isidore later returns to Moscow carrying the union’s decisions. The resulting rejection in Moscow becomes part of the author’s history of Russian ecclesiastical government. This supplies historical context for Mark’s stand, rather than making the nineteenth-century book a contemporary transcript of the debates. Its polemical descriptions remain the author’s Orthodox assessment; the biography does not infer that every Western Christian or every later Protestant personally accepted every disputed proposition.

blocks.text: The cathedral life names George Scholarios among his disciples and describes the later commemoration on January 19. Mark’s importance lies in theological witness and the reception of Florence, not in a martyrdom by execution.

blocks.text: Mouravieff’s narrative follows the reception of Florence beyond Italy and Constantinople, especially through Isidore’s return to Russia. Mark’s refusal is therefore one part of a wider disagreement about doctrine, authority, and reception. The source’s national and confessional perspective remains visible rather than becoming an anonymous verdict attributed to every historian.
